title: Caushawasha
summary: A Southold swamp name on Hashamomuk Neck, likely preserving a Native personal name within wetland boundary records.
why_this_matters: Caushawasha appears to preserve a Native personal name connected with a swamp on Hashamomuk Neck, rather than a simple translated landform term. The general marker is intentionally approximate, but the name still points to wetlands with springs, brooks, shelter, and foodways that mattered in Native life. Southold's swamp and neck landscapes are places of community memory and continued Indigenous presence, not empty land between better-known landmarks.
introduction_content: Caushawasha names a swamp on Hashamomuk Neck in Southold. It appears as a boundary place associated with the north side of the neck near Long Island Sound.
translation_content:
Caushawasha is treated as a personal name rather than a translated landscape term. English settlers often applied Native residents' names to swamps where people lived, especially places with springs, brooks, shelter, and nearby foodways.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place-names are first and foremost labels attached to one’s surroundings, as useful today as in prehistoric times.”

— Botolv Helleland, Place Names as Identity Markers (2011), Abstract
whereintheworld_content: Caushawasha preserves a named person, a swamp landscape, and a Southold boundary record together. The history also points to the importance of wetlands, springs, fields, and shell deposits in understanding lived Native places on the North Fork.
